patient.chief_complaint: Progressive headaches unresponsive to usual migraine treatment and behavioral changes over 2 months
patient.history_present_illness: This 44-year-old right-handed woman presents to the neurology service after referral from her primary care physician for evaluation of progressive headaches and behavioral changes over the past two months. The patient has a long-standing history of migraine without aura, typically experiencing 1-2 episodic throbbing headaches per month that respond well to sumatriptan and acetaminophen. Approximately eight weeks ago, the character of her headaches changed: they became more persistent, bilateral, with a pressure-like quality different from her usual migraines, and are notably worse in the morning upon awakening. On several occasions the headaches have woken her from sleep. Sumatriptan no longer provides relief, and over-the-counter analgesics are only partially effective. She initially attributed these symptoms to a recurrence of her chronic sinusitis, which had flared six weeks ago and was treated with a course of azithromycin. Despite completion of antibiotics, the headaches persisted and have progressively worsened. Over the past three weeks, her husband has noticed behavioral changes that he describes as out of character: she has become more irritable, occasionally short-tempered with her students at the high school where she teaches biology, and has twice forgotten to prepare lesson plans she had promised. She misplaced her car keys on three occasions and once could not recall the name of a colleague she has worked with for over a decade. These episodes have caused her significant distress, which she attributes to worsening anxiety. She also describes a vague, intermittent tingling sensation in her left hand and occasional clumsiness when writing on the whiteboard, which she has noticed over the past two to three weeks. Her husband witnessed one episode where she appeared to briefly stare blankly for about 10 seconds while cooking, after which she resumed her activity as if nothing had happened; she has no recollection of this event. She denies frank weakness, visual changes, difficulty swallowing, or gait instability. She denies fever, chills, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. Of note, she has a remote history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated at age 22 in Guatemala. Her sister was recently diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Her primary care physician ordered initial imaging, which revealed an intracranial abnormality prompting urgent neurology consultation and inpatient admission for further workup.

output.query: ring-enhancing brain lesion differential diagnosis MRI perfusion spectroscopy

results.title: Advanced MRI techniques for differentiating ring-enhancing brain lesions: A systematic review
results.summary: Perfusion MRI (rCBV) and MR spectroscopy improve specificity in differentiating GBM from abscess, lymphoma, and tumefactive MS. rCBV > 2.0 at enhancing rim strongly favors high-grade glioma. Restricted diffusion centrally is 95% specific for abscess. Elevated choline beyond enhancing margin is pathognomonic for infiltrative glioma.

results.title: Tumefactive demyelination vs. high-grade glioma: Imaging features and pitfalls
results.summary: Tumefactive MS shows incomplete (open) ring enhancement, lower rCBV (typically < 2.0), and a 'leading edge' of restricted diffusion. GBM shows complete ring enhancement (though may be irregular), higher rCBV, and choline elevation extending beyond enhancement. Family history of MS alone is insufficient for diagnosis.

results.title: CNS tuberculoma: MRI findings and differentiation from neoplasm in endemic regions
results.summary: Tuberculomas typically show ring or nodular enhancement, restricted diffusion centrally (caseous material), and associated meningeal enhancement. History of prior treated TB does not significantly increase risk for CNS tuberculoma decades later. MR spectroscopy showing a large lipid peak without elevated choline is characteristic of tuberculoma.

output.summary: Advanced MRI techniques (perfusion and spectroscopy) are highly effective in differentiating ring-enhancing brain lesions. Key distinguishing features: (1) High rCBV at enhancing rim (>2.0) favors high-grade glioma over abscess, lymphoma, and tumefactive MS; (2) Tumoral spectral pattern extending beyond enhancing margin is diagnostic of infiltrative glioma; (3) Restricted diffusion centrally strongly suggests abscess; (4) Tuberculomas show lipid peak without choline elevation; (5) Tumefactive MS shows incomplete ring enhancement and lower perfusion.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging mass effect (effacement of ventricles / sulci / cisterns): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Adequate pre-operative MRI characterization (mass, edema, eloquent-cortex proximity) is standard of care before neurosurgical tissue acquisition

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to control symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of intracranial mass effect — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right frontal lobe heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Mass effect, even when modest, makes lumbar puncture risky and low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis — MRI must precede any consideration of LP
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle due to multiple competing differentials: ring-enhancing lesion with incomplete enhancement pattern mimicking tumefactive demyelination, history of prior TB raising concern for tuberculoma, recent sinusitis with elevated inflammatory markers suggesting abscess, family history of MS and contralateral white matter lesion as red herrings. Correct diagnosis requires systematic use of advanced MRI (perfusion and spectroscopy) to exclude mimics and confirm infiltrative high-grade glioma.
